sJ9Ud7f3SYaU.text: To solve this problem, let's consider the penetrating ability of each subatomic particle

Xwm55wZagDMU.text: A good place to start would be searching for @penetrating power@, since this concept is related to the ability of subatomic particles to pass through matter

jYdXgPk3Q5Bc.text: Now, let's look at the properties of each subatomic particle:

F5zqqMdsPaTJ.text: - @beta particle@ is an electron emitted from the nucleus during certain types of radioactive decay

2sZMExkhgZ75.text: It has a relatively low penetrating power due to its small mass and charge

bDL9Ps6JuJrX.text: - @neutron@ has no charge and can penetrate materials, but its interaction with matter (mainly through nuclear scattering) limits its overall penetrating ability

iiZbNJqYgFcU.text: - @proton@ has a positive charge but a significant mass

Gv4NJjp5NdAp.text: Protons interact with charge-bearing particles and can be stopped in a thin layer of air due to ionization and nuclear scattering making them less penetrating than non-charged particles
